planning_principles: Exact Unit 1 Assessment Plan text controls section titles, Learning Targets, I-cans, vocabulary, representations, and misconceptions.
Canonical Bank WTC/Example/YTI content is referenced by exact IDs and is never rewritten in this map.

sections.learning_target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

i_cans.text: I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.
I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.
I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

story_beats.concept_title: Observations before explanations
story_beats.reading_goal: Establish the difference between what is directly observed or measured and what is inferred from those observations.
essential_ideas: Physics begins with observable events and measurements, not with labels attached after the fact.
An observation records what can be detected or measured; an inference interprets what those observations might mean.
Good models and explanations keep the evidence/interpretation boundary visible.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Treating an inference as an observation.
Assuming an explanation is scientific because it sounds plausible.
Treating a formula as a rule with no physical meaning.

story_beats.concept_title: Scientific ideas have different jobs
story_beats.reading_goal: Distinguish hypothesis, law, and theory by their role and connect scientific status to testability rather than certainty.
essential_ideas: A hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation or prediction.
A scientific law summarizes a consistent pattern or relationship; a scientific theory is a broad explanatory framework supported by evidence.
Scientific ideas remain open to evidence even when strongly supported.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Treating an inference as an observation.
Assuming an explanation is scientific because it sounds plausible.
Treating a formula as a rule with no physical meaning.

story_beats.concept_title: Evidence can support without proving
story_beats.reading_goal: Develop evidence-based judgment: what a data set supports, what it does not establish, and what additional measurement would test a claim.
essential_ideas: Evidence is relevant when it bears on the claim being evaluated.
A testable claim must make contact with possible observations or measurements.
One pattern can support an explanation without ruling out every alternative explanation.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Treating an inference as an observation.
Assuming an explanation is scientific because it sounds plausible.
Treating a formula as a rule with no physical meaning.

story_beats.concept_title: Models and formulas represent relationships
story_beats.reading_goal: Use a physical model/relationship as a compact description of measurable quantities rather than an answer-producing rule.
essential_ideas: A model selects important features of a physical situation.
A formula states a relationship among quantities and can support prediction in more than one direction.
Variables and ratios have physical meanings that should be interpreted before calculation.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Treating an inference as an observation.
Assuming an explanation is scientific because it sounds plausible.
Treating a formula as a rule with no physical meaning.

story_beats.concept_title: From measurement to explanation
story_beats.reading_goal: Synthesize the section by tracing a defensible path from measurement to inference, model, testable claim, and evidence-based conclusion.
essential_ideas: Strong physics explanations make clear which statements are measurements and which are interpretations.
A model is useful when it can connect evidence to predictions that can be checked.
The same representation can contain observations, assumptions, and inferred relationships; students should identify which is which.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Treating an inference as an observation.
Assuming an explanation is scientific because it sounds plausible.
Treating a formula as a rule with no physical meaning.

sections.learning_target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

i_cans.text: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.
I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.
I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

Define inertia in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.
Define Newton’s First Law in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.
Define net force in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.
Define support force in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.
Define weight in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.

story_beats.concept_title: Motion does not need a continuing net push
story_beats.reading_goal: Build Newton’s First Law from the contrast between motion changing and motion remaining unchanged.
essential_ideas: An object keeps its state of rest or constant straight-line motion unless a net external force changes that motion.
Force is connected to change in motion, not to motion itself.
Predictions should begin by asking whether the net force is zero.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Assuming motion requires a net forward force.
Confusing no force with zero net force.

story_beats.concept_title: Inertia is a property, not a force
story_beats.reading_goal: Use familiar inertia demonstrations to separate an object’s resistance to changes in motion from an interaction force.
essential_ideas: Inertia describes the tendency of matter to resist changes in velocity.
Inertia is not an extra force that pushes an object forward.
Objects with matter have inertia whether they are moving or at rest.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Calling inertia a force.
Confusing no force with zero net force.

story_beats.concept_title: Support force and weight act on the same object
story_beats.reading_goal: Identify common vertical forces while keeping the modeled object/system explicit.
essential_ideas: Weight is the gravitational force on the chosen object.
A supporting surface can exert an upward support force on an object in contact with it.
A correct force model contains forces acting on the selected object, not forces that object exerts on something else.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Confusing no force with zero net force.

story_beats.concept_title: No forces is not the same as no net force
story_beats.reading_goal: Compare an ideal no-force situation with balanced nonzero forces and connect both to unchanged velocity.
essential_ideas: Several forces can act while their vector sum is zero.
Zero net force can describe an object at rest or one moving at constant velocity.
The presence of force arrows alone does not imply a change in motion; their vector sum matters.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Assuming motion requires a net forward force.
Confusing no force with zero net force.

story_beats.concept_title: Read force models through Newton’s First Law
story_beats.reading_goal: Synthesize force identification and motion prediction without inventing an inertia force.
essential_ideas: Name the object first, then identify external forces on it.
Determine whether those forces balance before predicting a motion change.
Use inertia as the property behind persistence of motion, not as a force arrow.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Calling inertia a force.
Assuming motion requires a net forward force.
Confusing no force with zero net force.

i_cans.text: I can explain why force is a vector quantity.
I can combine forces acting in the same direction or opposite directions.
I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.

Define direction in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.
Define resultant in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.
Define net force in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.

story_beats.concept_title: A force vector needs magnitude and direction
story_beats.reading_goal: Make arrow length and arrow direction carry explicit physical meaning.
essential_ideas: Force is a vector because both magnitude and direction are required to describe it.
A vector arrow is not decoration: its orientation encodes direction and its length can encode relative magnitude when a scale is defined.
Two forces with equal magnitudes can have different effects when directions differ.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Adding vector magnitudes without direction.
Treating arrow length as decorative.

story_beats.concept_title: Same direction adds; opposite direction competes
story_beats.reading_goal: Connect one-dimensional force arrows to a directed net-force result.
essential_ideas: Forces in the same direction reinforce one another.
Opposite-direction forces must be compared with direction preserved; the resultant points toward the larger total.
A zero resultant means the directional contributions balance.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Reversing the resultant direction.

story_beats.concept_title: The resultant is the single equivalent vector
story_beats.reading_goal: Read a vector diagram as a model and identify the resultant magnitude and direction from its geometry/scale.
essential_ideas: The resultant summarizes the combined effect of multiple force vectors.
For collinear forces, the resultant follows signed/directed addition; for simple perpendicular vectors, geometry can represent the combined direction and magnitude.
The resultant must preserve both magnitude and direction.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Adding vector magnitudes without direction.
Reversing the resultant direction.

story_beats.concept_title: Work backward from a target net force
story_beats.reading_goal: Use a desired resultant to infer the missing force while maintaining direction conventions.
essential_ideas: A missing force can be determined by treating the target resultant as a constraint.
The unknown arrow must be chosen so all vectors combine to the required net force.
Reasonableness can be checked by reconstructing the vector sum.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Adding vector magnitudes without direction.
Treating arrow length as decorative.
Reversing the resultant direction.

story_beats.concept_title: Vector models must be read, not just calculated
story_beats.reading_goal: Synthesize vector meaning, arithmetic, and diagram interpretation through comparison of alternative force arrangements.
essential_ideas: A correct numerical magnitude with the wrong direction is not a correct vector result.
Scale and direction information in a diagram are evidence, not decoration.
Students should be able to move between arrow models and verbal statements about the net force.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Adding vector magnitudes without direction.
Treating arrow length as decorative.
Reversing the resultant direction.

sections.learning_target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

i_cans.text: I can recognize static equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.
I can explain why an object at rest can still have forces acting on it.
I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.

vocabulary_development.definition_target_before_summary: Define mechanical equilibrium in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.
Define static equilibrium in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.
Define dynamic equilibrium in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.
Define balanced forces in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.
Define constant velocity in section-specific physics language and connect it to the representation/evidence job where it first appears.

story_beats.concept_title: Equilibrium is a net-force condition
story_beats.reading_goal: Define mechanical equilibrium through zero net force, then distinguish static and dynamic cases by motion evidence.
essential_ideas: Mechanical equilibrium means the vector sum of forces is zero.
Static equilibrium describes an object at rest with zero net force.
Dynamic equilibrium describes constant straight-line motion with zero net force.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Equating equilibrium with rest only.
Assuming constant speed always means equilibrium even when direction changes.
Assuming forces disappear at equilibrium.

story_beats.concept_title: Rest can include real forces
story_beats.reading_goal: Use a balanced support situation to reject the idea that forces disappear when an object is at rest.
essential_ideas: An object can be motionless while several forces act on it.
At rest in equilibrium, opposing force components balance so their sum is zero.
Force existence and net-force value are different questions.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Equating equilibrium with rest only.
Assuming forces disappear at equilibrium.

story_beats.concept_title: The equilibrium rule can reveal a missing force
story_beats.reading_goal: Use Sigma F = 0 as a relationship that constrains unknown force components in a balanced situation.
essential_ideas: For equilibrium, upward and downward components balance and leftward and rightward components balance.
A missing force can be inferred from the requirement that each directional sum produces zero net force.
The relationship describes the physical condition; it is not merely an algebra step.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Equating equilibrium with rest only.

story_beats.concept_title: Constant straight-line motion can be equilibrium
story_beats.reading_goal: Connect constant velocity with zero net force and distinguish it from constant speed while turning.
essential_ideas: Dynamic equilibrium requires constant velocity, so both speed and direction remain unchanged.
A box moving steadily can have opposing nonzero forces whose net is zero.
Constant speed alone is insufficient if direction changes.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Equating equilibrium with rest only.
Assuming constant speed always means equilibrium even when direction changes.
Assuming forces disappear at equilibrium.

story_beats.concept_title: Use motion evidence to test a force model
story_beats.reading_goal: Synthesize equilibrium by checking whether the force model and the described motion tell the same story.
essential_ideas: A force diagram predicting zero net force should agree with rest or constant straight-line motion.
If the force components do not balance, the object is not in mechanical equilibrium.
Motion evidence can expose a force-model mismatch even before detailed calculation.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Equating equilibrium with rest only.
Assuming constant speed always means equilibrium even when direction changes.

sections.section_title: Modeling Forces in the Real World
sections.learning_target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

i_cans.text: I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.
I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.
I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

story_beats.concept_title: Define the system before drawing forces
story_beats.reading_goal: Make object/system selection the first move in building a real-world force diagram.
essential_ideas: A force diagram represents forces acting on one selected object/system.
Every arrow should correspond to an external interaction with that object.
Forces the chosen object exerts on other objects do not belong on its force diagram.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Including forces that act on other objects.
Matching a force diagram to the wrong motion description.

story_beats.concept_title: Balanced or unbalanced comes from the vector sum
story_beats.reading_goal: Classify a model by comparing force components rather than by counting arrows.
essential_ideas: Balanced forces produce zero net force.
Unbalanced forces produce a nonzero net force with a direction.
Equal-looking arrow counts do not guarantee equilibrium; magnitudes and directions matter.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Including forces that act on other objects.
Matching a force diagram to the wrong motion description.

story_beats.concept_title: Net force predicts how motion changes
story_beats.reading_goal: Connect the direction of a nonzero net force to the direction of velocity change without assuming it must match current motion.
essential_ideas: A nonzero net force causes a change in velocity.
The net-force direction identifies the direction of the acceleration/change in velocity, not necessarily the direction the object is currently moving.
A model should be checked against the motion evidence in the scenario.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Matching a force diagram to the wrong motion description.

story_beats.concept_title: Critique the model, then revise it
story_beats.reading_goal: Develop a repeatable model-critique routine: define the system, inspect each arrow, check balance, compare with motion evidence, and revise.
essential_ideas: A flawed force model may include a force on another object, omit an interaction, use an inconsistent arrow, or conflict with the described motion.
Revision should fix the physical model, not merely relabel an incorrect arrow.
Physics vocabulary should describe why the revised model is more consistent with the evidence.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Matching a force diagram to the wrong motion description.

story_beats.concept_title: Force models are claims that must match evidence
story_beats.reading_goal: Synthesize the Unit by treating a force diagram as a model that must be internally consistent and consistent with observed motion.
essential_ideas: The modeled object, force arrows, net force, and motion description form one connected explanation.
A representation mismatch is evidence that at least one part of the model or claim must be revised.
Students should justify revisions with named forces, balance/net-force reasoning, and motion evidence.
misconceptions_or_contrasts: Including forces that act on other objects.
Matching a force diagram to the wrong motion description.

generated_representation_needs.purpose: Provide a clean response surface for students to construct a force diagram without pre-drawing answer-bearing force arrows.
required_contents: room around object for student arrows and labels
optional neutral direction reference only if needed by the prompt
answer_neutrality_constraints: Do not pre-draw forces students must identify or determine.
Do not label support, weight, friction, tension, net force, or resultant unless the specific prompt supplies that information as a given.
Do not include a motion arrow if students must infer motion/change from the force model.

common_mistakes: Including forces that act on other objects.
Matching a force diagram to the wrong motion description.
